content: Oxcarbazepine is a keto derivative of carbamazepine, a medication commonly used as a mood stabilizer. It has been hypothesized to be effective in treating acute episodes of bipolar disorder, including mania, mixed episodes, and depression. Additionally, oxcarbazepine may have pharmacokinetic advantages over carbamazepine. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and acceptability of oxcarbazepine compared to placebo and other treatments for acute bipolar episodes. To achieve this, electronic databases were searched up to September 2, 2011. Hand searches of specialist journals and conference proceedings were also conducted. Experts in the field and pharmaceutical companies were contacted to obtain information on both published and unpublished trials. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared oxcarbazepine with placebo or other agents for the acute treatment of bipolar disorder. Participants of all ages and sexes with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder were included. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors. For dichotomous outcomes, odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, while continuous data were analyzed using standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% CIs. Seven studies involving a total of 368 participants were included in the analysis. These studies focused on mania, hypomania, mixed episodes, or rapid-cycling bipolar disorder. However, the overall methodological quality of the studies was relatively low. In one study involving children, there was no significant difference between oxcarbazepine and placebo in achieving a 50% or greater reduction in the Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) score (N=1, n=110, OR=2.10, 95% CI 0.94 to 4.73). No studies were available for adult participants comparing oxcarbazepine to placebo. When compared to valproate, oxcarbazepine showed no significant difference in antimanic efficacy, as measured by a 50% or greater reduction in YMRS scores (OR=0.44, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.97, 1 study, n=60, P=0.273) or by differences in YMRS scores between the two groups (SMD=0.18, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.59, 2 studies, n=90, P=0.40). No data were available comparing oxcarbazepine to lithium monotherapy for primary or secondary efficacy outcomes. As an adjunctive treatment to lithium, oxcarbazepine was found to reduce depression scores more effectively than carbamazepine in manic participants. This was demonstrated on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) (SMD=-1.12, 95% CI -1.71 to -0.53, 1 study, n=52, P=0.0002) and the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) (SMD=-0.77, 95% CI -1.35 to -0.20, 1 study, n=52, P=0.008). Participants receiving oxcarbazepine experienced a higher incidence of adverse effects, particularly neuropsychiatric side effects, compared to those receiving placebo. In one study (n=115), 17% to 39% of participants on oxcarbazepine reported at least one adverse event, compared to 7% to 10% of participants on placebo. However, there was no significant difference in adverse event rates between oxcarbazepine and other mood stabilizers or haloperidol. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence from high-quality trials to determine the efficacy and acceptability of oxcarbazepine for the acute treatment of bipolar disorder. Most studies focused on mania, with limited data on mixed affective states, hypomania, and rapid-cycling bipolar disorder. In children and adolescents, oxcarbazepine did not demonstrate superior efficacy compared to placebo. In adults, it was not more effective than other active agents. Oxcarbazepine may have a less favorable tolerability profile compared to placebo. Importantly, no data were available on clinically relevant outcomes, such as the duration of hospital admission. There is a need for well-designed, adequately powered randomized controlled trials to better understand the therapeutic potential of oxcarbazepine across the spectrum of acute bipolar episodes.
